title: Boss: review PR 512 from the CI plan
summary: Turn the checklist into a tool that lists every destroy in any plan JSON, then write the review that blocks PR 512, with the reason and the safe alternative for each blocker.

steps.title: PLAT-512
body: *"CI attaches the plan JSON to every pull request. Nobody reads 30 resources of tag changes, so destroys get
approved. Give us a script that lists what a plan destroys, and do the review of PR 512 with it."*
`~/review/PR.txt` describes the pull request, `~/review/plan.json` is the real plan CI made (the `hashicorp/aws`
provider, the same plan as in the lesson), and `~/review/aws-pr/` has the code before and after. Two steps.

steps.title: List what a plan destroys
prompt: Write `~/review/destroys.sh`: given a plan JSON file (`bash destroys.sh plan.json`), it prints the address of every
resource the plan **deletes**, one per line, sorted. A replacement deletes too, in either order (`-/+` is
`["delete","create"]`, `+/-` is `["create","delete"]`). A plan that deletes nothing prints nothing.
It is checked against `plan.json` and against other plans.

checks.name: PR 512's destroys, sorted
checks.cmd: cd ~/review && test "$(bash destroys.sh plan.json | tr '\n' ' ')" = "aws_db_instance.main aws_s3_bucket.assets aws_s3_bucket_versioning.assets "
checks.fail: `bash destroys.sh plan.json` should print `aws_db_instance.main`, `aws_s3_bucket.assets` and `aws_s3_bucket_versioning.assets`, one per line, sorted. Look at `jq '.resource_changes[] | {address, actions: .change.actions}' plan.json`.

checks.name: a plan without destroys prints nothing
checks.cmd: cd ~/review && jq '.resource_changes |= map(.change.actions = ["update"])' plan.json > /tmp/none.json && test -z "$(bash destroys.sh /tmp/none.json)"
checks.fail: On a plan where every action is `update`, the script printed something. Read the actions from the file you are given (`$1`), do not hard-code addresses.

checks.name: create-before-destroy counts as a destroy
checks.cmd: cd ~/review && jq '(.resource_changes[] | select(.address == "aws_instance.web") | .change.actions) = ["create","delete"]' plan.json > /tmp/cbd.json && bash destroys.sh /tmp/cbd.json | grep -qx aws_instance.web
checks.fail: A `+/-` replacement (`["create","delete"]`) also destroys the old object: test whether the actions *contain* `delete`, not whether they start with it.

hints: Each entry of `.resource_changes` has an `.address` and `.change.actions`, an array such as `["update"]` or `["delete","create"]`.
`select(.change.actions | index("delete"))` keeps the entries whose actions contain `delete`, wherever it is.
steps.explain: Three of the nine changes destroy something, and none of them is what the PR title says. A script like this runs in CI on every plan and posts its output on the PR, so a reviewer starts from the destroys instead of finding them on page three.

steps.title: Write the review
prompt: Write the review of PR 512 in `~/review/REVIEW.md`. Its first line is the verdict: `Request changes`.
Then one comment per blocker, each naming the **address**, the **reason** the plan gives, and the **safe
alternative**: the database (which attribute forces the replacement, and what happens to the data given
`skip_final_snapshot`), and the assets bucket and its versioning (why they are destroyed, and the fix). Then the
update that needs a maintenance window because of downtime: name its attribute.
Use the plan, not the PR description: `jq` on `plan.json` gives you every name you need.

checks.name: the verdict
checks.fail: The first line of `~/review/REVIEW.md` should be `Request changes`.

checks.name: the database blocker
checks.fail: Name `aws_db_instance.main`, the attribute that forces its replacement (`jq '.resource_changes[] | select(.address == "aws_db_instance.main") | .change.replace_paths' plan.json`), and what the missing final snapshot means for the data.

checks.name: the bucket blocker
checks.fail: Name `aws_s3_bucket.assets` and `aws_s3_bucket_versioning.assets`, where they went (`module.assets...`), and the fix (`moved` blocks).

checks.name: the maintenance window
checks.fail: Which update has downtime? Compare `.change.before.engine_version` and `.change.after.engine_version` of the database.

hints: `jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | index("delete")) | "\(.address) \(.action_reason // "") \(.change.replace_paths // [] | tostring)"' plan.json` gives each blocker with its reason.

`delete_because_no_resource_config` is the bucket: it is not in configuration any more, because it is `module.assets.aws_s3_bucket.this` now. `replace_paths` `[["storage_encrypted"]]` is the database.

The safe alternatives: encryption as its own migration (snapshot, encrypted copy, restore, cut-over) with `deletion_protection` on; two `moved` blocks for the bucket. The window: `engine_version` 16.4 to 17.2.
solution: echo '1. Blocking: aws_db_instance.main is replaced (-/+): storage_encrypted false -> true forces replacement, and with skip_final_snapshot = true and deletion_protection = false the production data is deleted without a snapshot. Do the encryption as its own migration (snapshot, encrypted copy, restore, cut-over).' >> REVIEW.md

echo '2. Blocking: aws_s3_bucket.assets and aws_s3_bucket_versioning.assets are destroyed (not in configuration) and created again as module.assets.aws_s3_bucket.this and module.assets.aws_s3_bucket_versioning.this. Add two moved blocks so the plan says has moved.' >> REVIEW.md
echo '3. Schedule: engine_version 16.4 -> 17.2 is a major upgrade with downtime; apply it in the maintenance window.' >> REVIEW.md
steps.explain: Every comment names an address, quotes the plan and gives the safe path: that is what lets the author fix it without a meeting. Compare with the fixed plan in the lesson: `0 to destroy`, the bucket *has moved*, the database updated in place with `deletion_protection` on.
